title: The LORD's Appointed Feasts
summary: God sets out Israel's sacred calendar: the weekly Sabbath, then the annual feasts of Passover and Unleavened Bread in spring, the waving of the first sheaf, the Feast of Weeks fifty days later, and in the seventh month the day of trumpet blasts, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lives in booths to remember the wilderness. Each is a sacred assembly with rest from ordinary work and offerings to the LORD.
story: After chapters on holy people (the priests) and holy things (the offerings), the Holiness Code turns to holy time. Israel's year was to be shaped around remembering what God had done and thanking him for what he gave. Several of these feasts appear elsewhere in the Torah (Exodus 12, 23, and 34; Numbers 28 and 29; Deuteronomy 16), but this chapter gathers them into a single calendar and adds details found nowhere else, such as the sheaf of firstfruits and the command to live in booths. It reaches back to the rescue from Egypt and forward to the harvests of a land Israel had not yet entered.
historical:
The feasts follow the farming year of the land of Israel, which is why verse 10 begins "When you enter the land". The months were lunar, beginning with the new moon. The first month (later called Nisan) falls in March or April, when the barley harvest begins; the Feast of Weeks came at the wheat harvest in late spring; and the seventh month (later called Tishri), in September or October, closed the year's harvest of grapes, olives, and other fruit. A small limestone tablet found at Gezer in 1908, usually dated to about the tenth century BC, lists the agricultural months in a similar sequence, showing how thoroughly Israel's life was tied to seasons of sowing and reaping.

Passover, Weeks, and Tabernacles became the three pilgrimage feasts, when Israelite men were to appear before the LORD at the sanctuary (Exodus 23:14-17; Deuteronomy 16:16). In the time of Jesus, Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims at each of them. Some details became matters of dispute. The phrase "the day after the Sabbath" (verses 11 and 15) was read by the Pharisees as the day after the first day of Unleavened Bread, whatever the day of the week, and by the Sadducees as the Sunday after the weekly Sabbath, which affected when Weeks was counted. The first day of the seventh month later became Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, though Leviticus calls it only a day of rest announced by trumpet blasts. After the return from exile, Nehemiah 8:17 records a celebration of booths on a scale not seen since the days of Joshua.
cultural:
Each feast joined memory and harvest. Passover recalled the night of rescue from Egypt, when the LORD passed over the houses marked with a lamb's blood and the destroyer did not enter them (Exodus 12:23), and the week of unleavened bread recalled the haste of leaving. The first sheaf of barley, waved before the LORD, acknowledged that the whole harvest was his gift, and no one could eat the new grain until it had been given. Fifty days later came the Feast of Weeks, with two loaves of leavened bread, the ordinary bread of daily life. The Greek-speaking Jews later called it Pentecost, meaning fiftieth. In between, verse 22 repeats the law of leaving the field's edges for the poor and the foreigner, so that the harvest festival would never forget those who had no harvest of their own.

The autumn feasts were the high point of the year. The Day of Atonement (chapter 16) was a solemn fast, but five days later came the most joyful feast of all. For seven days families lived in booths, temporary shelters made of branches, and rejoiced before God. Later Jewish practice identified the fruit of majestic trees in verse 40 as the citron, and waved it with palm, myrtle, and willow branches. Living in a flimsy shelter at the end of the harvest, with barns full, reminded Israel that they had once lived in the wilderness with nothing but what God provided.
literary: The chapter is a calendar arranged in five speeches, each opened by the LORD speaking to Moses (verses 1, 9, 23, 26, 33). The heading of verses 2 and 4 names the subject ("the LORD’s appointed feasts"), and verses 37 and 38 close it with a summary, before a supplement on Tabernacles (verses 39 to 43) adds the booths and the reason for them. The number seven runs through the whole: the seventh day, seven days of Unleavened Bread, seven weeks to Pentecost, the seventh month with three feasts, seven days of Tabernacles. The repeated phrases "sacred assembly" and "you must not do any regular work" mark each feast as holy time, set apart as the Sabbath is.

outline.t: Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread
The Feast of Weeks, and gleanings for the poor

doctrines.note: The spring and autumn feasts turn the harvest into worship. By giving the first sheaf and celebrating the final ingathering, Israel confessed that rain, growth, and bread come from God, not from their own labor alone.

Passover and Tabernacles tie the year to the exodus. Israel's identity rested on a rescue God had accomplished, and the calendar made each generation relive it, so that "your descendants may know" (verse 43).
The Day of Atonement stands in the calendar between the trumpets and Tabernacles. The year's great joy came only after the year's sins had been confessed and cleansed.

words.note: Mo'ed, an appointed time or festival. The word comes from a root meaning to appoint or meet, and it is related to the name of the Tent of Meeting. The feasts are God's appointments, times set by him for meeting with his people, not holidays of Israel's own making.

Miqra, a sacred assembly or convocation, from the verb to call. Each feast day is a day when the people are called together. The word occurs eleven times in the chapter and gives it a communal character: holiness here is kept together, not alone.

Bikkur, firstfruits: the first and best of the harvest, given to God. Giving the first portion acknowledged that the whole belonged to him and trusted him for the rest. Paul uses the Greek equivalent when he calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have died.

Sukkah, a booth or temporary shelter made of branches. The Feast of Tabernacles is in Hebrew the Feast of Sukkot, booths. The temporary shelter recalled the wilderness, where God sheltered his people with nothing more permanent than tents and a cloud.

christ: The New Testament connects several of these feasts to Christ. Paul writes, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Corinthians 5:7), and calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). The Gospels place Jesus' death at Passover and his resurrection on the first day of the week, which some Christians see as matching the waving of the first sheaf "on the day after the Sabbath" (verse 11), though the Gospels themselves do not draw that link. The Holy Spirit was poured out "When the day of Pentecost came" (Acts 2:1), fifty days after Passover. At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus stood and said, "If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink" (John 7:37), and John describes the incarnation with a verb related to pitching a tent: the Word "made His dwelling among us" (John 1:14). Some Christians also link the trumpets of the seventh month with the trumpet of Christ's return, but that connection is thematic, not something the New Testament states.

hard.q: Should Christians keep these feasts today?
hard.a: Christians have answered this in different ways. Most churches have held that the feasts, like the Sabbath regulations and sacrifices, were part of the Mosaic covenant fulfilled in Christ. They point to Colossians 2:16-17, where Paul tells believers not to let anyone judge them "with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath", calling these "a shadow of the things to come", and to Romans 14:5-6, where observing special days is left to conscience. Yet the church's own calendar grew out of this one: Easter is tied to Passover, and Pentecost keeps its name and place fifty days later. Other Christians, including many Messianic Jewish congregations and some Gentile believers, keep the biblical feasts as a way of honoring Jesus' own practice and seeing their fulfillment in him, though generally not as a requirement for salvation. Paul's warning in Galatians 4:10 against observing days applies, on most readings, to keeping them as a condition of acceptance with God. Jewish communities, of course, continue to keep these feasts as part of their covenant life.

questions: Israel's calendar was built around remembering what God had done. What rhythms in your week or year help you remember, and what crowds that memory out?
The harvest feast included a command to leave food for the poor. How could your own celebrations make room for those who have less?
The Feast of Tabernacles asked people with full barns to live in fragile shelters for a week. What might help you remember your dependence on God when life is secure?
